title: two Error classes whose durable contract identities used to be folded onto one string now mint two, and the program compiles
notes: specification/failures.mdx:209 (Locked): 'Handler selection MUST use compiler-stable nominal identity, not a forgeable user _tag or minifier-sensitive constructor name in compiled artifacts.' Read across the durable boundary (specification/durable-execution.mdx: 'Every value crossing an Action or Flow persistence boundary MUST satisfy the compiler-checked durable codec contract'), an identity is the key a decoder on the far side selects a handler by, so stability without INJECTIVITY is worthless: two declared Error classes arriving under one identity is precisely a forgeable key. WHAT THIS CASE WAS, AND WHY IT TURNED OVER. Until 2026-08-28 it was `two-error-classes-whose-durable-identities-collide-are-rejected`, and it pinned SMITHERS4124 on this exact program. The verdict was right for the identity the compilers had: the contract spelling was `smithers:<file>#<Class>@1` with every character outside [A-Za-z0-9._/@:+-] rewritten to `_`, so the `#` SEPARATOR was destroyed on every input and `$` folded onto `_` — `$Failed` and `_Failed` both minted `smithers:<file>__Failed@1` on BOTH backends, with the compiler reporting nothing until the union forced the refusal. The identity now escapes each component reversibly (`+0024Failed` vs `_Failed`) and withholds `@` from the alphabet so neither component can spell the separator, which makes the algorithm injective and this program ordinary. The case therefore moved from the refusing side of the line to the accepting side rather than being deleted: the specific pair that measured the defect is the one worth keeping as a regression guard, and a case that merely disappeared would leave nothing pinning that it compiles. WHY THE SPELLING IS PINNED NOW. Its predecessor deliberately did NOT declare the identity string, on the stated grounds that doing so 'would ratify that spelling as the contract and make the one-character repair a corpus break'. That repair has happened, so the reason not to pin it is spent, and this closes COVERAGE.md observation gap #15. Both backends were measured minting these bytes; they agree byte-for-byte here, as they do on the whole Plan for `an-actions-failure-channel-mints-one-identity-per-error-class`. WHY THE REFUSAL IS NOT RE-POINTED AT A STILL-COLLIDING PROGRAM. The residual no encoding can remove is two DIFFERENT declarations sharing (module, class name) — sibling namespaces are the smallest spelling — but that family is not filable here: the fork ALSO refuses it module-wide as SMITHERS1150, because its RUNTIME identity is a function of the same pair, while the reference has no module-wide equivalent and reports SMITHERS4124 alone. That is a both-closed divergence in reasoning, not a fail-open, and pinning it would freeze two unrelated rules against each other — the same reason the predecessor gave for leaving the same-NAME family unfiled. SMITHERS4124 keeps its direct coverage on both backends off-corpus instead: poc/src/durable/source-compiler.test.ts and compiler/fork_durable_identity_test.go both exercise the namespace channel and assert the refusal is live rather than dead code. WHERE THE ALGORITHM IS PINNED CROSS-BACKEND: conformance/identity/durable-failure-identity.json, 28 shared vectors read by poc/src/durable/durable-failure-identity.test.ts and compiler/fork_durable_identity_test.go. That file is the mechanism that stops the two copies drifting apart again, and it is a DIRECT assertion on purpose: both backends spelled this identity the same wrong way, so every cross-backend comparison in the tree agreed byte-for-byte on the colliding answer and this corpus reported `0 divergent` on the program above. A differential is blind to a defect both implementations share. THE PAIRED CASES: `two-error-classes-with-distinct-durable-identities-compile` holds the always-legal direction, and `an-actions-failure-channel-mints-one-identity-per-error-class` holds one-variant-per-class. Line 2 of this case's stdout is the obligation that can go to '1' if the fold ever returns; line 3 is the spelling; line 4 is injectivity stated as a set size, so a regression that re-folded the pair would fail lines 2, 3 and 4 together. SOURCE NARROWED 2026-08-28, expectation unchanged. `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` became enforced (compatibility.mdx §Mandatory, previously unimplemented), and this program read an index without narrowing, so it was correctly refused. §Mandatory's own guidance is that such a read 'MUST be narrowed, or read through an extraction helper'. The narrowing is inert at run time — the guard never fires — so the stdout this case pins is byte-for-byte what it was, re-derived by running both backends. ACCESSOR MOVED 2026-08-31, expectation unchanged. This case read the action count off `Flow.plan.actions`; it now reads it off `Flow.manifest.actions`. The reason is not cosmetic: `MIGRATION-PLAN.md` step 11 makes the Effect Manifest the artifact the Flow descriptor always carries, while the Plan is present only while the legacy lowerer can still hold the body and is retired with `plan-ir.ts` at step 12. Reading the action set off the Plan left the Manifest's action row unpinned by the corpus on the ACCEPTING side, which is the side the pivot moves everything to. Both backends were measured minting the same count through the new accessor; the declared stdout is byte-for-byte what it was, so what moved is where the number is read from and not what the number is.
